edition.title: Slow Burn - Sunday 8 November 2026
edition.fact: Edition 34. Bombs and envoys. Sunday 8 November 2026, edition 34. This edition runs 4,459 words. Happy Diwali: the Muhurat session opens Samvat 2083 today at 2:20 PM, with fourteen straight sessions of foreign buying behind it. Overnight the Gulf did two things at once - explosions sounded across Iran's Gulf coast hours after Washington disabled a blockade-running cargo ship and unveiled a task force to seal Iran's land routes, while Qatar's two-step peace plan, a letter from the US vice president and a call to Beijing all pushed the other way. Dhanteras gold sales ran to about Rs 60,000 crore, up 15-20% by value. Microsoft folded its frontier-research lab into a scaling-only organization, and the man who built it wrote the obituary. Israel's president tapped Netanyahu's rival to form a government. The long read is Haldiram's - the bhujia shop that told PepsiCo no.
edition.intro: The 5-minute lead route is first; sections carry the detail. The long read, for the Diwali table: a boy in Bikaner's Bhujia Bazaar, three cousin-kingdoms, a trademark war, the refusal of PepsiCo, and the Rs 84,000-crore reunion with Singapore's money inside.

blocks.html: Today's long read: The bhujia that said no - how Haldiram's grew from a contested 1918 start into three territorial family companies, fought a fifteen-year trademark war, refused every buyer from PepsiCo to Blackstone, merged its two biggest branches, and sold 9% to Temasek at an Rs 84,000-crore valuation. Read it here.
The session: Muhurat trading today - pre-open 2:05 PM, continuous 2:20-3:30 PM - opens Samvat 2083; eight of the last ten Muhurat sessions closed green.

The escalation: explosions were heard in Qeshm, Jask, Sirik and Bandar Abbas on Saturday evening, hours after US forces disabled the cargo ship M/V Huda and stood up a task force to disrupt Iran's land supply routes; Iran said two tankers struck mines in the strait.

The talks: Qatar's two-step plan - blockade lifted and frozen assets released for nuclear inspectors, the strait reopened on day two - sits with Tehran; Washington has asked Beijing to help, and Vice President Vance wrote to Iran's security chief.
The gold: Dhanteras sales came in at about Rs 60,000 crore, up 15-20% by value on roughly flat volume; silver rose 30% by value.
The lab: Microsoft merged its AI Frontiers research group into a scaling-first organization in September; its founder John Langford wrote the lab's farewell.
The government: Israel's president gave Gadi Eisenkot - not Benjamin Netanyahu - the first shot at forming a government, 67 endorsements to 46.
The long read: Haldiram's - the bhujia that said no.

1. The Muhurat session is today. The exchanges open this afternoon for the one ceremonial hour that starts the new Hindu financial year: pre-open at 2:05 PM, continuous trading from 2:20 to 3:30 PM on BSE, NSE and MCX, and with it Samvat 2083 begins (session times per the exchange circulars, via ET's guide). The session's record is a gambler's favourite statistic: Sensex and Nifty have ended eight of the last ten Muhurat sessions higher, with only 2016 and 2017 red (Economic Times). The market walks in on a run: seven straight winning sessions through Friday, the Sensex at 81,028.02 and the Nifty at 25,030.35, with foreign investors having bought for fourteen sessions straight - Rs 53,154 crore since 16 October (ET, on exchange data; index closes are BSE official). One count dispute, named: the same ET piece calls the recovery six sessions; this paper's count, from the exchange prints, is seven, and that is what we carry. The voices of the session: Religare's Ajit Mishra advises using Muhurat "to initiate selective positions in fundamentally strong companies rather than chase momentum"; ICICI Direct expects healthy double-digit returns in Samvat 2083, citing an improving earnings season and a Nifty two-year forward earnings multiple that has eased to sustainable levels after the correction; and Uday Kotak's Diwali message frames the year gone by as one of "geopolitics, AI, gold, oil, interest rates," notes that valuations have corrected and that about $700 billion of foreign portfolio money remains outstanding - hoping it stabilizes "as the overhang of excessive investment in AI corrects" (ET). Editor's takeaway: the session itself moves nothing - it is a ritual with a settlement slip - but the streak, the P/E reset and the $700 billion overhang are real, and Monday is the first full test of all three.

2. The shooting escalated overnight. Friday, US forces struck an Iranian air-defense installation - President Trump described it as minor: "they built a little bit of an antiaircraft device, and we knocked it out in about 15 minutes, maybe five" - the second strike on Iranian soil this week after Monday's, and the first since the midterm rout that cost Republicans both chambers of Congress (Los Angeles Times; Xinhua). Saturday escalated on three fronts. At sea, US Central Command said its aircraft fired precision munitions at the stern of the St. Kitts-flagged cargo ship M/V Huda in the Gulf of Oman after the crew ignored warnings to leave the area - the ship had visited an Iranian port and was breaching the blockade; CENTCOM's tally: 147 merchant vessels redirected since July, five disabled, and ten tankers of the IRGC's shadow fleet destroyed (Iran International's live blog). On land, CENTCOM announced a new task force to disrupt weapons shipments and illicit trade across Iran's land borders and the Caspian Sea - the blockade extended from sea to shore (Al Jazeera's live coverage). And on Saturday evening, explosions were heard across Iran's Gulf coast: state media reported blasts on Qeshm Island - two in its eastern part, per the IRNA agency - and in Jask, Sirik and Bandar Abbas; the cause is officially unclear, with a state television reporter suggesting Iranian defensive operations, while local media carried claims that two missiles struck Qeshm and that Iranian air defenses downed two US MQ-9 drones - claims this paper carries as claims, not confirmations (Al Jazeera; Xinhua). Iran's IRGC, for its part, said two oil tankers that attempted an unauthorized route through the strait hit naval mines and caught fire, and warned that vessels cooperating with the US military risk the same. Separately, CENTCOM is offering up to $20 million and possible relocation for information on Iran's nuclear program (Xinhua). Editor's takeaway: a ship disabled, a land task force, and unexplained blasts on four coastal points in one day is not de-escalation - whatever the diplomacy says, the military tape is still running, and the first thing to watch is whether anyone claims the Qeshm explosions.

3. The diplomacy intensified at the same time. The plan on the table is Qatar's, and its shape is now public: in step one, the US lifts the Hormuz naval blockade and releases part of Iran's $8 billion in frozen assets while Iran admits IAEA inspectors to its bombed nuclear sites - on the basis of the abandoned September 2025 Cairo agreement - and in step two, on day two, Iran reopens the strait; down-blending Iran's highly enriched uranium is an option, and no removal commitment is required up front (The Guardian). The obstacles are named: Tehran distrusts the IAEA's Grossi, accusing him of failing to criticize the US bombing and fearing inspection data could target future strikes. Around the plan, an unusual crowd of intermediaries worked the phones this weekend: Qatar's emir spoke with Trump on Friday (the Guardian); Washington has asked Beijing to help end the war and China conveyed the message to Tehran, the Washington Post reported, with Vice President Vance leading the effort - including a letter proposing renewed talks to Iran's security chief (Iran International); Iran's SNSC secretary Mohsen Rezaei met President Putin in Moscow on Thursday carrying a message from Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei; Foreign Minister Araghchi called his counterparts in Oman, Jordan, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Türkiye and Kuwait; and Iraq's foreign minister proposed a regional committee to shuttle between Tehran and Washington (Xinhua). Inside the White House, the Wall Street Journal reports the advisers are split: military leaders favor further strikes, while Vance and envoy Steve Witkoff pursue the deal (Iran International). Qatar's prime minister said mediation continues despite a slowdown, and that American willingness to pursue a deal survived the midterms - Vance himself has said the war, not just its cost, was critical to the Republican collapse (The Guardian). Editor's takeaway: both tapes are running at full speed - the strikes and the shuttle - and oil, which just had its worst week of the war on hope alone, reopens Monday with the Qatar plan unanswered and four coastal cities echoing; the plan's contents and Washington's reply are the conditions to watch.

4. Dhanteras bought the dip, in gold. India's festival gold demand held its value through the correction: preliminary estimates from the Gem and Jewellery Council put Dhanteras gold sales at about Rs 60,000 crore, up 15-20% from last year by value on roughly flat volume, with silver up 30% by value and 10% by volume (GJC's Rajesh Rokde to PTI, via CNBC-TV18). Footfalls were higher, said the council's vice-chairman Avinash Gupta, with buyers favouring lightweight pieces, smaller coins and lower carats - Delhi's 24-carat rate stood at about Rs 1.46 lakh per 10 grams including taxes on Friday, after the recent correction. Editor's takeaway: flat volume at plus-20% value is the price doing the work, not new buyers - India bought the same amount of gold for more money, which is what an inflation hedge looks like from the inside.

5. Eisenkot gets the nod in Jerusalem. President Isaac Herzog on Saturday gave Gadi Eisenkot - the former military chief and Benjamin Netanyahu's main rival - the first mandate to form Israel's next government, after the October 27 election left no one able to govern alone (Iran International). The final results: Netanyahu's bloc won 53 seats, the main opposition bloc 48, and Arab-led parties 19 (AP). In the endorsement count, Eisenkot drew 67 of the Knesset's 120 members - including the Arab parties - against Netanyahu's 46; the catch is structural, since Eisenkot has refused to form a coalition with those same Arab parties, which complicates his path to a majority. He now has 28 days, with a possible 14-day extension from Herzog, while Netanyahu remains prime minister through the negotiations (Iran International). The new Knesset holds its inaugural session on Tuesday (Anadolu). Editor's takeaway: 67 endorsements against a self-imposed refusal to seat some of them is a puzzle, not a majority - watch which centrist and right-wing doors open for Eisenkot before the 28 days start shrinking.

No session on Saturday; the reference closes remain Friday's: Sensex 81,028.02 (+2.17%) and Nifty 25,030.35 (+2.01%), a seventh straight winning session, with India VIX up 13.35% on Friday (BSE official closes, carried from edition 33). Today's Muhurat session runs 2:20-3:30 PM with a 2:05 PM pre-open; its print lands after this paper's deadline and will be covered tomorrow. Oil reopens Monday with Brent at $98.32, down more than 16% on the week, and the Gulf tape moving in both directions (story 2 and 3 above).

New to the pipeline: IL JIN Electronics (India), the electronics-manufacturing arm of Amber Enterprises, filed its draft red herring prospectus with SEBI on Saturday - dated 6 November - for a Rs 2,500-crore IPO, following Amber's 11 July intimation of the plan (NDTV Profit; the DRHP is the pre-price document - see today's term). Repro stands at Friday's close of Rs 313.10 (no Saturday session). The EAAA bond (10.8%, BSE symbol 108EAAAL27): still no verified close in the data this desk uses; Thursday's verified print was 109,619, a 9.6% premium to face value - the line returns when a verified close exists. Still on file: Anthropic's amended S-1, with third-quarter financials public, remains the overseas filing to read (carried from edition 32).
With no Saturday session, Friday's verdicts remain the live board going into the Muhurat hour (all BSE official closes, carried from edition 33):

blocks.html: New York's Friday finals, carried: S&P 500 7,376.86 (+0.31%, week -2.7%); Dow 51,285.73 (-0.46%, week -0.9%); Nasdaq 24,579.42 (+1.09%, week -3.4%, still in correction). Oil: Brent settled $98.32 (week -16%+); WTI $90.83 (week about -13%).

Nothing new landed over the holiday weekend in the verified record. Standing items: Infosys's Rs 26 interim dividend pays out on Wednesday 11 November. Bosch's 3:1 bonus plus 1:5 split approved Friday awaits the postal ballot; record date still to be fixed. ONGC's Rs 8 interim dividend was declared with Thursday's print.

The arithmetic of a Dhanteras. The council's headline is Rs 60,000 crore, up 15-20% - but the volume line says India's gold appetite did not grow at all: roughly the same weight of metal changed hands as last year (GJC estimates, via CNBC-TV18). Divide value by volume and the entire rise is price - buyers paid more per gram for the same grams, and chose lighter pieces and lower carats to keep their budgets intact. Silver is the sharper signal: value up 30% on volume up 10% means both price and quantity rose - silver is still being accumulated, gold is being maintained. The behaviour has a name in every jeweller's ledger: when the ritual spend is fixed in rupees, a price rally shows up as thinner bangles, not empty shops. Meanwhile the streak ledger pauses over the holiday weekend exactly where Friday left it - fourteen sessions, Rs 53,154 crore of net foreign buying since 16 October (ET, on exchange data) - with the Muhurat hour and Monday's first full session of Samvat 2083 as the next two entries.

No new verified startup print landed in the holiday window, so this section says so rather than dress up stale wires. The week's scorecard stands as printed: one pass - Lenskart, which held its post-results move at Rs 724.70 on Friday - and two sells, Nykaa and Honasa, both punished despite near-double profit growth; the multiple, not the growth, is still doing the talking (BSE official closes, carried). The pipeline's next hard date is not a startup at all but a corporate carve-out: IL JIN Electronics' Rs 2,500-crore DRHP, filed Saturday, is the document to read when SEBI's observations come back (story in IPOs).

Microsoft closed the lab that was supposed to find the next thing. In 2023, after ChatGPT, a group inside Microsoft Research organized AI Frontiers - about fifty people - to do coherent, fast frontier work: the Autogen orchestration framework, the Fara computer-use agent, the Next Latent objective, the Dion3 optimizer, the Full Bandwidth Transformer, and a monorepo shared across MSR that carried a proven edge-scale pretraining codebase (John Langford's own account). In early September the group was folded into Microsoft AI - the much larger organization built on the ex-Inflection leadership - and Langford, its founder, has now written the epitaph: MAI's core philosophy is "scaling, and aggressively not research," a choice he calls understandable from a business seat - "returns to scale are far more predictable than returns to research" - and personally "misdirected and not fun"; the evidence, he writes, was that "they just did not really want us." Indian coverage frames the post as Langford quitting. Read it beside this paper's thread from Friday: Microsoft reportedly stepping back from neocloud partners while CoreWeave - reporting Tuesday - carries the buildout's borrowed money. Editor's takeaway: the same company is now economizing on both the landlords of the AI buildout and the researchers of the frontier - two separate retreats from unpredictability, and the capex reappraisal has reached the lab door.

Langford's post is a research obituary, but buried in it is a builder's gift: predictability. "Returns to scale are far more predictable than returns to research" is an admission by the people spending the billions that model capability will now improve on a schedule - smooth, financed, and boring. A builder cannot plan around a breakthrough, but can absolutely plan around a schedule. So the practical rule this desk takes from Microsoft's choice: design your stack as if next year's model will be twice as capable at half the price, because someone has now budgeted exactly that. Own what does not depreciate - your data, your evaluations, your user's workflow - and hold loosely what does: prompts tuned to one model's quirks, scaffolding that exists only because the model is weak today. Research made the models surprising; scaling makes them infrastructure. Build for infrastructure.

If your family trades the Muhurat session, do it the way the ritual intends: at 2:20 PM, buy the one share you decided on last night, in the amount you would gift, and log off by 3:30. The trade is real - it settles like any other - so keep it token; the session's value is the shagun, not the fill. And at the Diwali table tonight, when the sweets come out, check the packet: there is a fair chance it is Haldiram's, and now you know the story - the boy who doubled his grandfather's price, the cousins who split the map, and the family that told PepsiCo no. The long read is here.

The new year that begins at 2:20 PM today is Samvat 2083 - the count of the Vikram Samvat calendar, the Hindu era whose year number runs fifty-seven ahead of the Gregorian one (2,083 minus 2,026). For most of India it is a calendar; for the markets it is an accounting year. Trading families and brokers traditionally close their ledgers on Diwali, worship the new account books - the chopda pujan - and open the fresh year with the first auspicious transaction, which is what the exchanges' Muhurat session formalizes into an order book (ET, on the Samvat 2083 session). So when brokers forecast "Samvat 2083 returns," as ICICI Direct does today, they mean the stretch from this Diwali to the next - a year measured lamp to lamp, not January to December. The convention is old enough that it prices nothing and frames everything: the scoreboard that resets this afternoon is the one Dalal Street actually watches.

A draft red herring prospectus is the first public document of an IPO - the version a company files with SEBI before it can sell anyone a share. "Draft" because SEBI's observations can still force changes; "red herring" from the old American warning legend, because the two things investors care most about - the price and the dates - are deliberately not in it. What is in it: audited financials, the business's risks in the company's own words, who the promoters are, and what the money is for. IL JIN Electronics filed its DRHP, dated 6 November, with SEBI on Saturday: Rs 2,500 crore, out of Amber Enterprises' manufacturing arm (NDTV Profit). The sequence from here is SEBI's observations, then the red herring prospectus proper with a price band, then the issue. When someone says a company "filed for an IPO," the honest reading is: the paperwork exists, the price does not. Everything before the RHP is intention.

Sunday's board is a carry-forward: no Saturday session, and today's one-hour Muhurat trade - symbolic by design, thin by tradition - does not activate setups; Monday is the next scored session. The desk's rule stands: every published setup stays on the board until it completes (target hit) or fails (stop hit). Per-share prices on every line; the Rs 1,500 price cap screens what qualifies as a setup. Ledger: Slow Burn swing research, 24 Oct.

blocks.html: The resolved line stays in the ledger: HCLTech, filled 28 October at the worst fill of Rs 1,378.00, target Rs 1,466.80 taken out at Friday's high of Rs 1,468.00 - gross +6.44%, net +6.14% after the 0.3% cost convention, in seven sessions; the stop at Rs 1,346.90 never traded. Of the open lines: Kotak (Rs 480.00) has held above its Rs 437.55 trigger for ten sessions - a candidate, not a setup. ONGC (Rs 232.00) spent a fourth session above 228 inside its Rs 218.50-238.75 coil, carrying an Rs 8 dividend and a 47% consolidated profit print against a crude price that fell 16% on the week - the coil decides, and Monday's oil reopen feeds it directly. Infosys (Rs 1,180.65) sits inside the Rs 1,175 trigger zone with Wednesday's Rs 26 payout ahead. JSW Steel (Rs 1,359.00) keeps failing the published R:R screen, which is why it stays a watchlist line. Hindalco (Rs 957.70) is the new candidate: momentum (closed at the day high after a 5% intraday shakeout), heavy results-day volume, and the strongest quarter in its history - but no entry zone until levels are verified against a longer price history. Voltas stays rejected (fell 2.43% on its own beat); Tech Mahindra stays shelved above the cap.

blocks.html: Three conditions, in the order they resolve. First, today's Muhurat hour and Monday's first full session of Samvat 2083: fourteen sessions and Rs 53,154 crore of foreign buying meet a holiday tape and a reopen - whether the bid keeps arriving in size, or shrinks back to the run's average day, separates conviction from crowding. Second, the Gulf's two tapes: explosions on four coastal points and a new land-blockade task force on one side, Qatar's two-step plan, the Vance letter and the Beijing channel on the other - what matters next is whether the Qeshm blasts get claimed, whether Washington answers Doha formally, and how Monday's oil reopen prices a plan that exists alongside live strikes. Third, Jerusalem's 28-day clock: Eisenkot's 67 endorsements include parties he refuses to seat - watch which doors actually open once the new Knesset is sworn in on Tuesday. This desk does not predict the answers; it watches these conditions.

The Gulf's two tapes. Cause chain: months of naval blockade; a Qatari peace plan taking shape; oil's worst week of the war on hope; then Friday's strike on an air-defense battery, Saturday's disabling of the M/V Huda, a new task force to seal Iran's land routes, evening explosions along the Gulf coast - and, in parallel, the Qatar two-step plan going public, a Trump-emir call, a Vance letter to Tehran's security chief, and a Chinese channel opened. Watch next: any claim of responsibility for the Qeshm blasts, Washington's formal reply to the plan, UKMTO incident reports, Monday's oil reopen. Proven wrong if: a signed agreement lands while ships are still being disabled and struck.

The FII streak. Cause chain: foreign investors sold Indian equities through most of 2026; since 16 October they have bought fourteen sessions straight - Rs 53,154 crore - with domestic funds selling into the bid throughout; Uday Kotak's Diwali message puts $700 billion of foreign portfolio money as the overhang to watch. Watch next: the Muhurat hour's provisional prints and Monday's flows. Proven wrong if: the daily foreign number flips negative and stays there while the indices sit near the week's highs.

The AI retrenchment. Cause chain: Thursday's Nasdaq correction priced the political risk to the data-center buildout; Friday brought reports that Microsoft plans fewer neocloud partners; Saturday added Langford's account that Microsoft has folded its frontier-research lab into a scaling-only organization - cost discipline reaching the research budget. Watch next: CoreWeave's third-quarter print on Tuesday - contracted capacity and capex guidance, not the share price - and any Microsoft confirmation of either retreat. Proven wrong if: hyperscaler capex guidance rises through the correction and frontier research keeps getting funded at the frontier firms that matter.

items.detail: Diwali (Lakshmi Puja). Muhurat trading opens Samvat 2083: pre-open 2:05 PM, continuous session 2:20-3:30 PM on BSE, NSE and MCX (exchange circulars via ET).

items.title: Mon 9 Nov
items.detail: First full Indian session of Samvat 2083 - the FII streak's fifteenth-session test. Oil reopens after its worst week of the war with the Qatar plan unanswered and strikes continuing.

items.title: Tue 10 Nov
items.detail: CoreWeave reports third-quarter results at 5:00 PM ET - the first neocloud print since the correction (company IR announcement). Israel's new Knesset holds its inaugural session (Anadolu).

items.title: Watching
items.detail: Any claim for the Qeshm explosions; Washington's reply to the Qatar plan and UKMTO incident reports; Eisenkot's coalition soundings on the 28-day clock; Nvidia reports 17 November; Bosch's postal ballot; SEBI's observations queue for IL JIN's DRHP.

items: Sources read for this edition: Los Angeles Times on Friday’s strike and the M/V Huda; The Guardian on the Qatar two-step plan and the emir’s call; Al Jazeera’s live blog on the coastal explosions and the land-routes task force; Iran International’s live blog for the CENTCOM tally, the Washington Post and Wall Street Journal reporting it carried, and the Eisenkot mandate details; Xinhua for the IRGC statements, the drone and missile claims, the $20 million reward and the diplomatic calls; AP for the final Israeli seat counts; Anadolu for the Knesset date; Economic Times for the Muhurat session, the Samvat voices and the FII streak; CNBC-TV18 for the GJC Dhanteras estimates; John Langford’s own post on AI Frontiers; NDTV Profit on the IL JIN DRHP; CoreWeave’s own IR announcement for the Tuesday print time; BSE’s official bhavcopy behind every Indian price carried from Friday.

Corrections discipline: the Indian winning streak is carried at seven sessions from exchange prints - the Economic Times’ "six-session recovery" is named in story 1 as a conflict, not merged. The cause of Saturday evening’s explosions is officially unclear; the two-missiles and two-drones lines are carried as Iranian local-media claims via Xinhua, not as confirmed events. The M/V Huda’s flag and the CENTCOM tallies are as CENTCOM stated them. The Temasek stake in the long read is 9% per the deal reporting; one profile rounds it to 10%. Haldiram’s founding year is contested - 1918, 1919 and 1937 are all named where they appear rather than resolved silently. The EAAA bond has no verified close and says so. A Bajaj Finance "results" item circulating Saturday was dropped: the company reported on 23 October and the new items are business-update rewrites. Anything later than about 6:45 AM IST is deliberately not in this edition.
